Canada.polity: Hunter-gatherer and fishing peoples (Dorset Paleo-Inuit in the eastern Arctic, Plains bison hunters, Northwest Coast societies)
Canada.summary: No states or writing; everything known comes from archaeology. The eastern Arctic was home to the Dorset Paleo-Inuit, then in their Late Dorset period; the early Inuit (Thule) arrived only centuries later. On the northern Plains, bison hunters had used the bow and arrow since about 200 CE. Northwest Coast peoples lived in permanent settlements built on salmon and cedar, with considerable wealth and political complexity.

events.t: Late Dorset period (from c. 500): Dorset exchange networks span the eastern Arctic, though they have left Newfoundland and much of southern Labrador.
On the northern Plains, bison hunting with the bow and arrow, associated with the Avonlea people since about 200 CE, continues.
Northwest Coast peoples live in permanent settlements supported by salmon runs and cedar, without farming.

sources.title: Geographic Distribution of the Dorset Culture

United States of America.polity: Diverse Native American societies (Late Woodland, Basketmaker III Ancestral Puebloans, Hohokam, Weeden Island and others)
United States of America.summary: No states, cities or writing. In the East, Late Woodland peoples (c. 600–900) built fewer burial mounds and long-distance trade declined, but the bow and arrow and new crop varieties spread and sites multiplied. On the Colorado Plateau, Basketmaker III Ancestral Puebloans farmed and lived in pithouse villages. Hohokam farmers lived along the Salt and Gila rivers. Weeden Island villages in north Florida and Georgia built mounds.

events.t: Late Woodland period begins in the Southeast: Middle Woodland mound building and long-distance trade decline, while settlements become more numerous.
The bow and arrow spreads in the East and replaces the atlatl among Ancestral Puebloans; new varieties of maize, beans and squash gain importance.
Basketmaker III Ancestral Puebloans (settled at Mesa Verde from c. 550) live in pithouse villages, farm corn, beans and squash, and make pottery.
Hohokam farming villages occupy the Phoenix Basin along the Salt and Gila rivers, a culture famed for extensive irrigation canals.
Weeden Island I culture (c. 250–700) in north Florida and south Georgia: villages with mounds, charnel houses and elaborate ceremonial pottery.

Mexico.polity: Teotihuacan in decline; Maya kingdoms such as Palenque and the Kaanul (Snake) kingdom
Mexico.summary: Teotihuacan, once the largest city in the Americas, had its major buildings deliberately burned around 600 and lost its regional dominance, though people kept living there. In the Maya south, the Kaanul (Snake) kingdom, then based at Dzibanché, attacked Palenque in 599 and again in 611. Pakal, born 603, became king of Palenque aged twelve in 615. In the 630s the Kaanul royal seat shifted to Calakmul.

events.t: Kaanul (Snake) forces from Dzibanché attack Palenque; the attack is credited to the Kaanul king Sky Witness, though this placement is chronologically puzzling.
Teotihuacan's major buildings are deliberately burned and sculptures smashed; the city stays inhabited but loses its regional dominance.
K'inich Janaab Pakal, the future king of Palenque, is born.
The Kaanul king Scroll Serpent attacks Palenque, the second Kaanul assault there, as recorded in Palenque's Temple of the Inscriptions.
Muwaan Mat becomes ruler of Palenque after the death of Aj Ne' Yohl Mat.
Pakal, aged twelve, becomes king of Palenque; he rules until 683.
After a Kaanul civil war (630–640), Yuknoom Ch'een II accedes as founder of a reconstituted Kaanul kingdom whose capital has shifted from Dzibanché to Calakmul.

sources.title: Table of Palenque Rulers

Guatemala.polity: Maya kingdoms (Tikal, Naranjo and others) under pressure from the Kaanul (Snake) kingdom and Caracol
Guatemala.summary: The Petén lowlands were divided among rival Maya kingdoms that recorded dynastic history in hieroglyphic inscriptions. Tikal's king Wak Chan K'awiil suffered a 'star war' defeat in 562, after which no monuments are known at Tikal for about 130 years. The Kaanul (Snake) kingdom and its ally Caracol dominated the region; Caracol attacked Naranjo from 626, and Naranjo fell in 631.

events.t: Tikal's long monument hiatus continues after its 562 defeat: no monuments are known there for about 130 years.
B'ajlaj Chan K'awiil, a Tikal prince who later rules from Dos Pilas and submits to Calakmul, is born at Tikal.
Caracol's king K'an II attacks Naranjo, the first of three assaults recorded for 626–627.
Naranjo is conquered; inscriptions credit Caracol's K'an II with a 'star war' and the Kaanul lord Yuknoom Head, aided by fighters from Calakmul, with its seizure.

Belize.polity: Maya kingdom of Caracol, ally of the Kaanul (Snake) kingdom
Belize.summary: Caracol was a rising Maya kingdom. Its inscriptions record the 562 'star war' defeat of Tikal, though the damaged victor's name on Caracol Altar 21 may be that of a Kaanul (Snake) king. Under K'an II, who ruled 618–658, Caracol repeatedly attacked Naranjo. Archaeology shows prosperity and rapid population growth at the start of the Late Classic period, when most of Caracol's causeways were built.

events.t: Caracol Stela 6 records the seating of a figure called Flame Ajaw for a bloodletting rite, during an interregnum before K'an II's accession.
K'an II, son of Yajaw Te' K'inich II, becomes king of Caracol; he rules until his death in 658.
K'an II's forces make the first of three attacks on Naranjo (626–627), recorded at both Naranjo and Caracol.
Caracol under K'an II defeats Naranjo in a 'star war', probably bringing it under his direct control.

sources.title: A. F. Chase and D. Z. Chase, The Materialization of Classic Period Maya Warfare: Caracol Stranger-Kings at Tikal
In search of the serpent kings: From Dzibanche to Calakmul

Honduras.summary: Copán, in western Honduras on the southeastern frontier of the Maya world, was a royal city whose dynasty traced its founding to K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', inaugurated in 426. With its subordinate centre Quiriguá, Copán controlled the Motagua River trade route. In 628 K'ahk' Uti' Witz' K'awiil, the 12th ruler, began a reign that lasted until 695.

events.t: K'ahk' Uti' Witz' K'awiil (also called 'Smoke Imix'), the 12th ruler, becomes king of Copán; he reigns until 695.

sources.title: Copan Monument Manual, Part 2 (Stela E)

El Salvador.polity: Maya and other farming communities (e.g., San Andrés, Joya de Cerén)
El Salvador.summary: The region had recovered from the huge Tierra Blanca Joven eruption of Ilopango, now dated to 431 ± 2 CE (it was once linked to c. 540). Ash-covered land was resettled once it weathered into fertile soil. San Andrés was reoccupied and urbanised, becoming the centre of the Zapotitán valley. Around 600 the farming village of Joya de Cerén was buried by the Loma Caldera eruption, preserving houses, fields and tools.

events.t: San Andrés, reoccupied after the Ilopango eruption (431 CE), grows into the political, economic and religious centre of the Zapotitán valley.
Loma Caldera erupts and buries Joya de Cerén, preserving buildings, maize fields and household goods (dated c. 600; also given as 590 ± 90).

Nicaragua.polity: Farming communities of the Greater Nicoya cultural area (Pacific side)
Nicaragua.summary: There were no states or writing, and everything known comes from archaeology. Pacific Nicaragua belonged to the Greater Nicoya cultural area. During the Bagaces period its potters made Tola Trichrome, painted pottery whose designs are closely linked to Carrillo Polychrome from neighbouring Costa Rica. The Caribbean side is little known.

events.t: Bagaces period: potters in Pacific Nicaragua produce Tola Trichrome painted pottery, linked in style to Costa Rican wares.

sources.title: Tripod Jar with Costumed Bat-Man (Carrillo Polychrome, Greater Nicoya, AD 500-800)

Costa Rica.polity: Ranked farming societies of Greater Nicoya, the central and eastern regions, and Greater Chiriquí in the south
Costa Rica.summary: Settlements grew in number and size, and rich elite burials show growing social distinctions, with contacts to Mesoamerica and Colombia. Jade carving, a status marker for a thousand years, died out (by about 700) as gold became the preferred prestige material. Polychrome pottery and finely carved effigy metates flourished. Near Arenal, villagers wore deep footpaths walking to distant cemeteries for generations. Evidence is archaeological.

events.t: Gold replaces jade as the main prestige material; Maya jade is still traded in and recarved (jade use ends c. 700).
Improved stone carving produces elaborate effigy metates with human, animal and composite figures.
Near Arenal volcano, generations of walking between villages and cemeteries such as Silencio wear footpaths metres deep.

sources.title: Central America and the Caribbean, 500–1000 A.D.
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

Panama.polity: Ranked societies of the Conte phase (central Panama)
Panama.summary: Central Panama was in the Conte phase (c. 500–800). Goldworking was fully established, and boldly drawn Conte polychrome pottery showed creatures perhaps linked to myth or cosmology. Elite burials grew richer: the El Hatillo cemetery came into use around 700, and the famous chiefly burial at Sitio Conte dates to about 750. There was no writing; all knowledge comes from excavation.

events.t: Conte polychrome pottery, boldly painted with mythical creatures, is made in central Panama, where goldworking is well established.

sources.title: Central America and the Caribbean, 500–1000 A.D.
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

Cuba.polity: Archaic (Casimiroid) peoples; Ostionoid farmers beginning to arrive in the east
Cuba.summary: Cuba had long been home to Archaic (Casimiroid) peoples whose ancestors came from Central America. From about 600, pottery-making Ostionoid farmers expanding from Hispaniola began to colonise eastern Cuba, the start of the line that led to the Taíno. Whether the Ostionoids grew mainly from Saladoid or from Archaic roots is debated. Little can be dated precisely.

events.t: Ostionoid peoples expanding through northern Hispaniola begin to colonise eastern Cuba; Archaic communities continue elsewhere on the island.

Bahamas.polity: Not yet settled, or only just being reached
Bahamas.summary: The Bahamas were the last part of the Caribbean to be settled. Ancestors of the Lucayans began colonising the Turks and Caicos and the Bahamas from about 600, coming from the Greater Antilles. The oldest sites, in the Turks and Caicos, suggest arrival by about 700; on Great Abaco, burning for farming appears around 830. Dates of first settlement remain debated.

events.t: Ostionoid seafarers from the Greater Antilles may be starting to reach the southern Bahama islands; secure evidence of settlement dates from c. 700.

Jamaica.polity: Probably uninhabited until the first Ostionan settlers in the 7th century
Jamaica.summary: Jamaica is believed to have been uninhabited until the 7th century, when it was colonised by Ostionan Ostionoids, probably moving along the south coast of Hispaniola. Known locally as the Little River Complex or 'Redware' people for their red pottery, they lived mainly near the coast and depended heavily on marine resources. Exact dates are uncertain.

events.t: First known settlers, Ostionan 'Redware' potters, colonise Jamaica in the 7th century (exact date uncertain).

Haiti.polity: Archaic (Casimiroid) peoples and expanding Ostionoid farmers
Haiti.summary: Western Hispaniola had long been home to Archaic (Casimiroid) peoples. By about 600, pottery-making Ostionoid farmers were expanding along both coasts of Hispaniola, the line that led to the Taíno. Their simple red-slipped Ostionan pottery is called redware. Scholars debate whether the Ostionoids derived mainly from Saladoid settlers or from local Archaic peoples. Detailed dates are scarce.

events.t: Ostionoid peoples expand westward along both coasts of Hispaniola, alongside long-established Archaic communities.

Dominican Rep..polity: Ostionoid farming villages and Archaic (Casimiroid) peoples
Dominican Rep..summary: Eastern Hispaniola was the western limit of the earlier Saladoid expansion, whose advance stalled there, perhaps because of established Archaic populations. By about 600, Ostionoid farmers with simpler red-slipped pottery were expanding across Hispaniola. These communities were ancestors of the Taíno whom the Spanish met. Whether they grew from Saladoid or Archaic roots is debated.

events.t: Ostionoid farming communities spread through Hispaniola from the east, beside older Archaic groups; Ostionoid origins are debated.

sources.title: The Native Peoples of Turks and Caicos
sources.publisher: Florida Museum of Natural History, Caribbean Archaeology Program

Puerto Rico.polity: Village societies in transition from Saladoid to Ostionoid
Puerto Rico.summary: Puerto Rico had been farmed for about a thousand years by Saladoid peoples from South America, who lived in villages around central plazas and made fine white-on-red pottery. Around 600, archaeologists see major social reorganisation and a shift to the Ostionoid tradition, named after the Ostiones site in western Puerto Rico, with plainer red-slipped pottery. Ball courts and plazas belong to this Ostionoid era and later Taíno society.

events.t: The Saladoid tradition gives way to the Ostionoid; pottery decoration simplifies and leadership and social status are reorganised.
Ball court and plaza sites begin in the Early Ostionoid period (c. 600–1200); centres such as Tibes develop over the following centuries.

Trinidad and Tobago.summary: Trinidad, near the Orinoco, lay on the route by which Saladoid pottery-making farmers spread from South America into the Caribbean. Saladoid and Barrancoid ceramic traditions are both found in Trinidad and Tobago in the period up to about AD 750, reflecting close ties with the mainland. Dating is approximate.

events.t: Villages in Trinidad and Tobago make pottery in the Saladoid and Barrancoid traditions, linked to the South American mainland.

Colombia.polity: Regional chiefdom societies (San Agustín, Tierradentro, San Jorge floodplain and others)
Colombia.summary: Colombia had chiefdom societies but no empire or writing. Around San Agustín in the upper Magdalena, the Regional Classic period (c. 1–900) saw elite burial mounds with stone tombs and large carved statues. At Tierradentro, monumental painted shaft-and-chamber tombs (hypogea) were cut into volcanic tuff from about 600. In the San Jorge floodplain of the north, ridges and canals managed floodwaters, with the region at its height c. 400–1000.

events.t: San Agustín's Regional Classic period (c. 1–900) continues, with burial mounds over stone tombs guarded by large carved statues.
At Tierradentro, communities begin cutting decorated underground tomb chambers (hypogea) into volcanic tuff (c. 600–900).
In the San Jorge floodplain, ridges and drainage canals manage seasonal floods; the region is at its height c. 5th–10th centuries.

sources.title: San Agustín Archaeological Park

Venezuela.polity: Village and early chiefdom societies (e.g. western Llanos of Barinas)
Venezuela.summary: There were no states or writing. The best-studied area is Barinas in the western Llanos and Andean piedmont. There, occupation was sparse in 300–550, but in the following phase (550–1000) the number of settlements rose sharply and chiefdoms with centralized authority began to form. Petroglyphs in the piedmont may mark a trade route between the Llanos and the high Andes. Knowledge is entirely archaeological.

events.t: In Barinas, settlements multiply (to 32 in the Llanos and six in the piedmont in 550–1000) and chiefdoms begin to form.

sources.title: Archaeology of the Western Venezuelan Llanos: The Barinas Project

Guyana.polity: Village societies of the coast and interior
Guyana.summary: Very little is known. In the northwest, coastal people of the Mabaruma phase, connected to Barrancoid traditions of the Orinoco, built shell middens and made pottery. Interior savanna and forest groups farmed manioc and fished. Dates are rough and the sites few.

events.t: Mabaruma-phase villages in northwest Guyana make Barrancoid-related pottery and farm manioc.

Suriname.polity: Village societies of the coast and interior
Suriname.summary: The record is thin and dates are broad. On the swampy coastal plain of western Suriname, people built raised fields (mounds and ridges with ditches and canals) linked to habitation mounds. According to Rostain, the first raised fields were made by migrants from the lower Orinoco from about 1,800 years ago, and the tradition later spread east into French Guiana. Knowledge is archaeological only.

events.t: Raised-field farming, introduced from the lower Orinoco from about 1,800 years ago, is practised on the western coastal plain.

sources.title: La mise en culture des marécages littoraux de Guyane à la période précolombienne récente (Stéphen Rostain)

Ecuador.polity: Regional coastal and highland societies (late Regional Development period)
Ecuador.summary: Ecuador had regional societies but no state. On the coast this was the end of the Regional Development period, which lasted until about 700; the Integration period that followed brought population growth and sharper social ranking. Spondylus shell, found off the warm Ecuadorian coast but scarce in Peru's cold waters, had great ritual value in the Central Andes, and Peruvian demand rose sharply after about 600.

events.t: Peruvian demand for Ecuadorian Spondylus shell rises considerably after Moche V (c. 600).
In southern Manabí, settlements stay small with little stratification until the end of the Regional Development period (c. 700).

sources.title: La trayectoria del desarrollo social precolombino en el sur de Manabí (Martín & Lara 2009)
sources.publisher: Antropología: Cuadernos de Investigación (PUCE), via Dialnet

Peru.polity: Late Moche polities (Pampa Grande), the expanding Wari state, late Nazca, Recuay; Tiwanaku colonies in Moquegua
Peru.summary: A time of upheaval. Severe droughts and El Niño floods strained the north-coast Moche; new inland centres such as Pampa Grande rose as the old southern capital declined. In the highlands, the Wari state was expanding from its capital near Ayacucho. Nazca culture was in its late phase on the south coast and Recuay persisted in the north highlands. Tiwanaku colonists from the Titicaca basin farmed the Moquegua valley.

events.t: Droughts and El Niño floods (dated c. 560–600 by some, c. 630 by others) strain the Moche; the southern capital at Moche is largely abandoned.
Pampa Grande (c. 550–700), with the huge Huaca Fortaleza platform, becomes the largest Moche city, in the Lambayeque valley.
Wari, north of modern Ayacucho, is a prosperous metropolis and capital of a rapidly expanding state, with specialized craft compounds.
Tiwanaku colonists from the altiplano farm the Moquegua valley, beginning with Omo-style settlements.
Late Nazca culture (c. 100–700) continues on the south coast; Nasca styles shape Wari's Chakipampa ceramics.

Bolivia.polity: Tiwanaku (Lake Titicaca basin); Casarabe culture in the Llanos de Mojos
Bolivia.summary: Tiwanaku, near the south shore of Lake Titicaca, was in its apogee (c. 500–900) as a ceremonial and political centre with monuments such as the Akapana, Kalasasaya and Pumapunku. Raised-field farming and lake resources supported it, and its influence reached colonies in Moquegua and Cochabamba and, through caravan trade, distant oases. In the Amazonian lowlands, the Casarabe culture (c. 500–1400) built platform mounds, causeways and canals.

events.t: A major construction programme begins at Tiwanaku, including the Akapana pyramid with seven stone-walled platforms and an expanded drainage system.
Monumental human-form stone sculptures, including the Bennett Stela, are erected at Tiwanaku.
The Casarabe culture (c. 500–1400) in the Llanos de Mojos develops settlements that later include platform mounds, raised causeways and canals.

Chile.polity: Atacama oasis communities linked to Tiwanaku; Bato and Llolleo horticulturalists in central Chile
Chile.summary: In the north, the San Pedro de Atacama oases were drawn into Tiwanaku's economic and ideological sphere, probably through caravan trade rather than conquest; Tiwanaku-style goods appear mainly in burials. In central Chile, Bato and Llolleo groups of the Early Ceramic period lived in the Santiago basin; Llolleo numbers grew after about 700 with greater reliance on maize. Knowledge is archaeological only.

events.t: San Pedro de Atacama burials include Tiwanaku-style textiles, drinking cups and hallucinogen paraphernalia, reflecting links with the Titicaca basin (c. 400–1000).
Bato and Llolleo horticultural groups occupy the Santiago basin during the Early Ceramic period (c. 200 BC–AD 1300).

Argentina.summary: In the northwest Andean valleys, the Aguada peoples built on earlier Condorhuasi-phase developments. Their gray and polychrome ceramics, incised with dragonlike creatures and staff-bearing figures, suggest they shared in a wider pan-Andean mythology; Aguada bronzeworking became highly developed somewhat later. There was no writing, and evidence is archaeological, with broad dates.

events.t: Aguada peoples of northwest Argentina build on Condorhuasi traditions, making incised ceramics with dragonlike creatures and staff-bearing figures.

sources.title: Central and Southern Andes, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

Paraguay.summary: Guaraní-ancestral groups, originating in southwestern Amazonia, were beginning to settle the Plata basin; the earliest Guaraní sites there date to about 500 ± 100 CE along the Upper Paraná River. They hunted, fished, gathered and grew maize, tubers, beans, squash and peanuts, made corrugated and painted pottery and often buried the dead in urns. Precise dates for this period are few.

events.t: The earliest Guaraní sites in the Plata basin, along the Upper Paraná River, date to about 500 ± 100 CE.

sources.title: At the Southern limit: the Arenal Central site and the Guaraní occupation of the Paraná Delta (Loponte et al. 2025)

Uruguay.polity: Mound-building groups of the eastern lowlands ('cerritos de indios')
Uruguay.summary: In the Laguna Merín lowlands of eastern Uruguay, people built earthen mounds known as 'cerritos de indios', a tradition dated from about 5,000 to 250 radiocarbon years ago. Older models saw the mound builders as specialised hunters; newer fish-bone evidence suggests fishing was also important. Evidence is archaeological only.

events.t: The cerrito mound-building tradition of the Laguna Merín lowlands (c. 5000–250 radiocarbon years BP) continues.

sources.title: Aproximación a la pesca indígena en las tierras bajas de la Laguna Merín (Bica-Méndez 2022)

Brazil.polity: Diverse Amazonian and highland societies (Marajoara, Acre geoglyph builders, southern proto-Jê and others)
Brazil.summary: On Marajó Island, the Marajoara (c. 300–1350) lived on large earth mounds, built fishponds, and made elaborate pottery and burial urns. In Acre, people used huge geometric ditched enclosures (geoglyphs) as ceremonial gathering places within long-managed forest. In the southern highlands, proto-Jê groups of the Taquara-Itararé tradition, ancestors of the Kaingang and Xokleng, built pit-house villages and earthworks. No writing; dates come from excavation.

events.t: Marajoara communities on Marajó Island live on raised mounds, manage fishponds and bury ancestors in decorated urns (c. 300–1350).
Geometric ditched enclosures (geoglyphs) in Acre are built and used sporadically as ceremonial sites (c. 2000–650 years ago).
Southern proto-Jê groups of the Taquara-Itararé tradition (c. 380 BC–17th century) live in pit-house villages in the southern highlands.

Falkland Is..summary: No settlement is known. Europeans arriving in 1690 found no people. A 2021 study found evidence of pre-European visits by Indigenous South Americans, probably short stays, most likely between about 1275 and 1420, though earlier dates cannot be ruled out. The only native land mammal was the warrah, a fox-like canid.

events.t: No settlement is known; the main evidence for human visits points to c. 1275–1420, centuries later.

sources.title: Evidence of prehistoric human activity in the Falkland Islands (Hamley et al. 2021)
